Abstract
Digital education often relies on disparate platforms for communication,
content delivery, live teaching, and assessment. Although these tools may
be individually effective, their separation creates fragmented workflows,
repeated context switching, and weaker institutional continuity. This thesis
presents EduVerse, an integrated educational web platform with a mobile
companion application, designed to consolidate these activities within a
governed, role-based environment for administrators, teachers, and students.
EduVerse provides a comprehensive suite of learning management
features, including content distribution, assessments, real-time collaboration
via live sessions and whiteboards, an AI agent, and an integrated
browser-based IDE. The web platform is built using Next.js, React,
and TypeScript, integrating Supabase for authentication and relational
data, AWS S3 for file storage, LiveKit for real-time communication, and
OpenRouter for AI services. EduVerse Mobile—developed with Expo
and React Native—extends the platform through selected high-frequency
workflows, including class overviews, chat, notifications, materials,
organization switching, and basic live-session participation.
The evaluation combines automated logic-level testing with engineering
verification during development. The automated suite completed with 76
passed tests, 0 failures, and 105 assertions across 10 test files, while shared
API reuse and modular feature enablement support consistent role-based
academic workflows across the implemented clients. Consequently, EduVerse

learning environments.

1.1 Project Vision
Digital transformation has made online systems central to communication,
teaching, assessment, feedback, collaboration, and daily academic follow-up.
As this dependence grows, the quality of a learning environment increasingly
depends on whether its capabilities operate as a coherent academic system.
EduVerse advances a vision of an integrated educational platform in
which related academic workflows remain connected within one governed
environment. The platform is designed to support continuity across learning
activities while preserving clear institutional control.
This vision extends beyond a single institutional model. EduVerse
is conceived as an adaptable academic environment that can support
universities, schools, online academies, bootcamps, tutoring centers, training
contexts, and open-learning communities while accommodating different
educational needs.
At its core, the vision is to provide a coherent and configurable academic
workspace in which learning, communication, assessment, and institutional
governance can coexist within a unified platform.
1.2 Problem Statement
Many educational workflows are currently distributed across separate
systems. One platform may be used for class communication and
sharing materials, another for live meetings and presentations, another
for collaborative whiteboard interaction, and another for programming
practice. Familiar examples include Google Classroom for announcements
and materials, Google Meet for live calls, Excalidraw-like tools for shared
whiteboard work, and LeetCode-like environments for coding exercises.
While each tool can be useful on its own, their separation introduces
repeated context switching, disconnected workflow stages, weaker continuity
between related academic tasks, and scattered responsibility for governance
and follow-up.
This fragmentation becomes more serious in multi-organization
educational settings. A platform must not only expose features; it
must also manage roles, permissions, memberships, public access rules, class
visibility, and the relationship between administrative governance and daily
learning activity. When these concerns are spread across unrelated services,

The problem also has a client-design dimension. Rich administrative

1.3 Project Motivations
EduVerse was motivated by the need to design academic continuity
and institutional control together. The project brings governance,
communication, assessment, and learning support into one adaptable
environment so that related workflows can remain coherent across different
educational contexts.

1.6 Project Scope and Boundaries
1.6.1 System Boundaries and User Roles
EduVerse operates through three principal human roles: Organization
Administrator, Teacher, and Student. The same person may hold more than
one role, and a user may belong to more than one organization. For that
reason, the system resolves access according to the selected organization, the
active role, class membership, and the current feature configuration rather
than by assuming that every user belongs to one fixed category.
This role structure defines an important project boundary. EduVerse
is not a general social platform in which all users share the same
permissions. It is a governed educational workspace in which visibility,
management authority, assessment control, and feature access are
deliberately differentiated.
1.6.2 Functional Scope
Within its implemented scope, EduVerse includes authentication,
organization access and membership, class management, materials,
chat, assignments, exams, results, notifications, live sessions, whiteboard
collaboration, an AI Agent, and an integrated coding workspace. It
also includes organization-level and class-level feature controls, extension
support, and optional public or open-learning access where those capabilities
are enabled.
This scope is not restricted to higher education alone. The same model
can be adapted for primary schools and kindergartens through narrower
feature selection and closer organization-level control, just as it can support
more specialized contexts such as technical courses, tutoring programs, or
open learning initiatives.
The class model is intentionally flexible. A class can support a
conventional course, but it can also be used for a narrower academic
purpose. For example, a class may function as a digital library space
dedicated mainly to sharing books and learning materials. This flexibility
shows that EduVerse is not restricted to one teaching pattern; it is
a configurable academic workspace that can be adapted to different
institutional uses.

1.6.3 Web and Mobile Client Scope
The EduVerse web application is the primary and most complete client. It
supports the broader administrative, instructional, and assessment workflows
that define the platform as a full educational system.
EduVerse Mobile already exists as a companion mobile application,
developed to extend selected platform features to mobile users. Its
scope is intentionally narrower than the web platform. The current
mobile implementation supports authenticated access, class summaries,
notifications, materials, class chat, organization switching, and basic
live-session participation. It is therefore best described as a companion
under active development rather than as a feature-complete replacement for
the web platform. Administrative workflows and several advanced learning
features remain mainly web-side.
1.6.4 Distinctive Features and Extensible Design
EduVersecombinescommunication, materials, livecollaboration, assessment,
AI assistance, and coding practice within a governed multi-organization
model.
Its extensible design is also central to the project. Supported features
can be enabled or disabled at organization level and, where supported,
refined further at class level. AI features can likewise be disabled when
an organization or a specific class considers them unsuitable. The same
underlying API model also creates reuse potential for future integrations or
companion clients, because core workflows are exposed through protected
shared routes rather than being hard-wired to one interface only.
Public access adds another important dimension. When enabled, public
organizations or public join paths can support broader sharing of educational
materials and more open learning participation, while still remaining under
organization-defined governance rules.

Chapter 2. Literature Review and Theoretical Framework 8
2.1 Introduction
This literature review establishes the conceptual and technical foundations
relevant to EduVerse and situates the project within existing approaches
to digital education. Because the platform combines several forms of
academic activity, its theoretical basis extends across digital learning
systems, communication and synchronous teaching, artificial intelligence in
education, access control, mobile learning, and extensible platform design.
Together, these areas provide the basis for examining how educational
activities can remain coordinated while supporting different users,
institutional requirements, and modes of participation. The review
also identifies limitations in fragmented educational environments and the
design principles that motivate a more connected approach.
2.2 Evolution of Digital Education
Platforms
2.2.1 From Traditional Classroom Management to
Digital Learning Systems
Educational management has gradually moved from paper-based and
face-to-face coordination toward persistent digital systems capable of
organizing materials, communication, submissions, and academic records
at institutional scale. Learning management systems emerged as part of
this transition, providing shared digital spaces through which teaching and
learning could be organized more consistently [4, 3].
This transition also changed user expectations. Students and teachers
increasingly expect continuous access, asynchronous participation, traceable
communication, and structured academic follow-up rather than isolated
interactions [4]. Modern educational platforms are therefore evaluated not
only by their ability to store resources, but also by how effectively they
support ongoing academic activity.

2.2.2 Limitations of Fragmented Learning
Management Tools
Research on educational digitalization shows that institutions commonly
rely on combinations of specialized systems for learning management,
communication, synchronous teaching, collaboration, and practical work.
Although individual tools may perform their intended functions effectively,
using multiple disconnected environments can weaken continuity across
academic activities and increase coordination overhead [3, 11].
Such fragmentation can require users to repeatedly move between
separate contexts while institutions manage permissions, visibility,
communication, and responsibility across different services. The resulting
challenge is maintaining consistent academic coordination when related
activities are distributed across separate tools [3, 11].
2.3 Research Gap and Integrated Learning
Ecosystems
The gap relevant to EduVerse concerns coordinated operation across
individual educational tools. Existing systems can support communication,
learning resources, assessment, synchronous teaching, collaboration, and
practical work independently; however, institutions also require these
activities to operate within consistent boundaries of responsibility, access,
and academic context.
This creates a broader requirement for educational environments that

EduVerse addresses this gap by adopting an integrated but configurable

2.4 Artificial Intelligence in Education
Artificial intelligence has become increasingly relevant to education because
it can support explanation, summarization, drafting, and personalized
academic assistance when used within appropriate pedagogical boundaries
[2, 6]. Its educational value, however, depends not only on its ability to
generate content, but also on how its use affects teacher judgment, academic
integrity, and the learner’s engagement with source material.
For EduVerse, this literature supports treating AI as a supplementary
learning capability rather than as a replacement for instructional authority
or established academic resources.
2.4.1 Context-Aware Learning Assistance
AI assistance is generally more useful when it is informed by the learner’s
current academic context. Responses related to the active class, learning
material, or task can provide more relevant support than generic answers
detached from the educational setting [1, 6]. Context awareness can therefore
improve both relevance and pedagogical alignment.
This principle supports the use of embedded AI assistance in EduVerse,
where learning support is intended to remain connected to the academic
environment in which it is requested.
2.4.2 Material Summarization and Learning Support
Long or numerous educational resources can make it difficult for students
to quickly recover the structure and key ideas of a topic. AI-supported
summarization can assist by foregrounding important concepts and reducing
the effort required to re-enter complex material [14].
Such summaries should remain supportive rather than substitutive. In
the context of EduVerse, summarization is therefore treated as an aid for
navigating learning material rather than as a replacement for the original
resource.
2.4.3 Assessment and Feedback Support
The literature indicates that AI can contribute to formative learning support,
drafting, and feedback-related activities when used within clear educational

boundaries [6]. At the same time, unrestricted use can weaken authentic
assessment and blur the distinction between assistance and task completion
[9, 6].
These concerns support a cautious role for AI within EduVerse.
AI-assisted learning should complement teacher-led assessment and study
activities without replacing instructional authority or undermining the
integrity of assessed work.

2.6 Theoretical and Technical Foundations
of EduVerse
The preceding literature identifies several principles relevant to the design
of an integrated educational environment. The following subsections
summarize the foundations most directly related to EduVerse, including
web-based educational systems, mobile companion applications, synchronous
learning, integrated programming environments, extensibility, access control,
and data management.
2.6.1 Web-Based Educational Platforms
Web platforms remain central to comprehensive educational systems
because they can support rich administrative interfaces, detailed authoring
workflows, and persistent academic records. Their value lies not only in

Chapter 2. Literature Review and Theoretical Framework 13
browser accessibility, but also in their capacity to accommodate complex
institutional and instructional activities within a consistent interface.
These characteristics support the use of the web as the primary client
for comprehensive EduVerse workflows, while more focused forms of
participation can be extended through other clients.
2.6.2 Mobile Companion Learning Applications
Mobile educational applications are often most effective when they support
frequent and lightweight participation rather than reproduce the full
complexity of a comprehensive academic platform. Notifications, quick
updates, access to materials, communication, and entry into live activities
are examples of interactions that align naturally with mobile usage [12].
This literature supports the companion-client model adopted by
EduVerse, in which mobile access extends selected educational interactions
while the web application retains broader functional depth.
2.6.3 Real-Time Virtual Classrooms
Synchronous online teaching remains important because it supports
immediacy, responsiveness, and a stronger sense of instructional presence
[7]. Its educational effectiveness, however, is influenced by how well the live
activity remains connected to the wider learning context.
For EduVerse, this principle supports embedding synchronous
participation within the class environment rather than treating a live
session as an isolated event disconnected from communication, materials,
and subsequent academic activity.
2.6.4 Integrated Coding Environments for
Programming Education
Programming education illustrates the cost of fragmented digital workflows
particularly clearly. When explanation and practical coding are separated
across unrelated environments, students must repeatedly switch between
learning and execution contexts. Integrated coding environments can
reduce this separation by bringing practical work closer to the surrounding
instructional activity [10].

Chapter 2. Literature Review and Theoretical Framework 14
This principle supports the inclusion of browser-based coding within
EduVerse as a way of maintaining a closer relationship between programming
practice and the wider learning context.
2.6.5 Extensible Educational Ecosystems and
Governed Openness
Educational institutions rarely require every available capability in every
learning context. Modular platform approaches address this variation by
allowing functionality to be combined without forcing a rigid all-or-nothing
structure [13]. Extensibility is most useful, however, when it remains subject
to clear institutional control.
The same principle applies to openness. Broader access to learning
resources or participation can be valuable when visibility and authority
remain governed by institutional rules [11]. These principles support
EduVerse’s configurable approach without requiring every organization or
class to operate identically.
2.6.6 Security, Roles, and Data Management
Role management is a foundational requirement in educational systems
because students, teachers, and administrators interact with academic
information from different positions of responsibility. Role-Based Access
Control provides an established approach for separating permissions and
responsibilities among different actors [5].
This principle supports the role-aware access model used by EduVerse,
where academic and administrative actions are differentiated according to
the user’s institutional context.
Data management is equally important. Educational systems must
preserve academic records, protect sensitive information, and provide
structured access to learning materials and results [8, 5]. These requirements
provide the theoretical basis for treating data protection, controlled access,
and academic-history preservation as core system concerns.
Together, these foundations establish the academic and technical
rationale for EduVerse as an integrated educational platform. The literature
indicates that effective digital learning environments depend not only on
individual capabilities, but also on how communication, participation,
assessment, access control, and learning support are coordinated. The next
chapter builds on these foundations by presenting the methodology used to
analyze, design, implement, and refine the system.

Chapter 3. Methodology 16
3.1 Introduction
EduVerse combines multiple academic and administrative workflows that
share user roles, data, permissions, and interaction rules. Developing these
capabilities therefore required a methodology that could accommodate
progressive refinement while preserving consistency across the wider
platform.
Because dependencies between features often became clearer during
implementation and testing, the development process needed to support
repeated analysis, refinement, and integration rather than rely on a single
fixed development sequence.
3.2 Methodological Approach
EduVerse was developed using a hybrid iterative methodology with a mainly
feature-based vertical-slice approach. Development was organized around
individual academic and administrative features. Each feature was analyzed,
implemented across the required system layers, tested, and refined before
being integrated with the wider platform. This iterative process allowed
requirements and implementation details to be adjusted as development
progressed.
3.2.1 Iterative Feature-Centered Development
Development was organized around meaningful functional capabilities rather
than around isolated technical layers. Each iteration focused on a selected
academicoradministrativefeatureandmoveditthroughanalysis, interaction
design, implementation, testing, and integration.
This feature-centered organization kept development tied to recognizable
user or institutional outcomes while still allowing the required technical work
to span multiple system layers. One completed increment could also reveal
requirements or dependencies that informed the planning and refinement of
subsequent work.
The iterative process also supported coordination between the primary
web application and the mobile companion application. Features intended
for mobile use were refined across both applications, while more extensive
administrative and teaching workflows remained mainly on the web.

Chapter 3. Methodology 17
3.2.2 Vertical-Slice Realization
A feature was generally treated as a coherent functional unit rather than
divided into separate interface-only or backend-only development stages.
Depending on its scope, a feature slice could involve user interaction, business
rules, APIs, permissions, and persistent data.
For example, workflows such as assignment submission or examination
scheduling require more than an interface change because their behavior also
dependsontheactinguser, governingrules, andstoredacademicinformation.
The approach was predominantly, rather than exclusively, vertical.
Some features required changes across several system layers, while others
involved only a subset of those layers or extended into the mobile companion
application. The methodology therefore favored complete functional paths
where appropriate without requiring every increment to modify every layer
of the system.
3.2.3 Why This Methodology Fits EduVerse
A rigid sequential methodology was less suitable for EduVerse because many
platform capabilities share permissions, data, user context, and interaction
rules. Implementing and examining related functionality in practice clarified
these dependencies progressively.
An iterative approach allowed these dependencies to be addressed
progressively. Testing and refinement provided opportunities to identify
inconsistencies in workflows, permissions, interfaces, and data behavior
before each feature became fully integrated with the surrounding platform.
The vertical-slice emphasis complemented this iterative process by
keeping development focused on functional user outcomes rather than
isolated technical components. This was particularly useful in a multi-role
system where related workflows may behave differently for Organization
Administrators, Teachers, and Students.
3.3 Repeated Development Cycle
Each development increment followed a repeated six-stage cycle, with the
depth of each stage adjusted according to the feature and the system layers
involved. A relatively localized change could require limited supporting

4.2 System Overview
EduVerse is a multi-organization educational platform in which the class acts
as the primary operational workspace. The system supports three principal
human roles: Organization Administrator, Teacher, and Student, while the
same account may belong to multiple organizations or hold more than one
role.
System behavior depends on the active organization, active role, class
membership, and applicable feature configuration. These conditions
determine which resources, workflows, and management actions are available
to the current user.
The web application provides the primary operational environment,
while the mobile companion extends selected high-frequency academic
interactions. This chapter analyzes the system at the level of actors,
requirements, permissions, and workflows rather than implementation
architecture.

The principal human actors of EduVerse are the Organization Administrator,
Teacher, and Student. These roles represent different levels of responsibility
within the platform rather than permanently separate account types. A user
may belong to more than one organization or hold more than one role, with
access resolved according to the current workspace context. The diagrams

Chapter 5. System Design 61
5.1 Introduction
System design translates the analytical requirements established in the
previous chapter into a structured model for the organization of EduVerse.
This chapter presents the architectural context, information model,
relational database structure, and interface design principles that connect
users, academic workflows, data, and configurable access.
Theemphasisisplacedonhowthemajorpartsofthesystemareorganized
and related at design level, while the technical realization of these decisions
is discussed separately in the implementation chapter.
5.2 Design Context and Architectural
Structure
EduVerse is designed as a coordinated educational platform in which
related academic and administrative workflows operate within a shared
organizational and class context. The architecture separates the main
user-facing clients from persistent data, file-handling services, and real-time
communication capabilities while preserving common access and governance
rules.
The web application serves as the primary interface for comprehensive
academic and administrative workflows, while the mobile companion extends
selected forms of participation. Persistent academic and organizational data
are managed through the relational data layer, and specialized services
support capabilities such as uploaded learning resources and synchronous
sessions.
This structure allows individual services to remain technically distinct
while presenting users with a coherent educational environment governed by
shared organizational, role, class, and feature context.
5.3 Information Model and Persistence
Design
The EduVerse information model represents the relationships between
organizations, users, roles, classes, learning resources, assessments,
communication, and configurable platform capabilities. The database

Chapter 5. System Design 62
design supports these relationships while preserving the separation between
organization-level governance and class-level academic participation.
This section presents the logical database structure, the Entity
Relationship Diagram (ERD), and the principal schema groups required to
support the system at design level.
5.3.1 Logical Database Design
EduVerse uses a relational data model organized around the relationship
between organizations, users, and classes. The organization forms the
primary institutional context, while the class represents the main academic
workspace.
Organization membership is separated from class membership so that
institutional roles and class participation can be managed independently.
This distinction supports users who participate in multiple organizations,
hold different roles, or belong to multiple classes.
Academic entities such as materials, communication records, assignments,
examinations, notifications, and live sessions are associated with the relevant
organization and class context. Configuration entities are maintained
separately from ordinary academic content so that feature availability
and institutional settings can be applied without changing the underlying
learning records.
The resulting model supports multi-organization governance, role-aware
access, class participation, academic history, assessment workflows, and
configurable feature availability within one relational structure.
5.3.2 Relational Structure Through the ERD
The Entity Relationship Diagram provides the central design-level
representation of the EduVerse data model. It shows how institutional,
academic, and configuration entities relate to one another and clarifies the
cardinalities that connect users, organizations, classes, learning resources,
assessments, and platform settings.
The model includes direct one-to-many relationships as well as
many-to-many relationships resolved through intermediate membership or
configuration structures. These relationships are important because users
may participate in multiple organizational and academic contexts rather
than belonging to one fixed system role or class.

Chapter 5. System Design 63
Principal Relationship Structure
•Organization and membership structure.Organizations
provide the institutional context for memberships, classes, settings,
invitations, and configurable capabilities. User membership records
connect individual accounts to the organizations in which they
participate.
•Role structure.Membership and role relationships allow access
responsibilities to be represented within an organization context rather
than assigning one permanent platform-wide role to each user.
•Class participation structure.Classes belong to organizations,
while class-membership relationships connect users to the academic
workspaces in which they participate. This resolves the many-to-many
relationship between users and classes.
•Learning and communication structure.Materials and
communication records are associated with classes so that learning
resources and class interaction remain tied to the appropriate academic
context.
•Assessment structure.Classes contain assignments and
examinations, with related submission, question, attempt, and
answer records representing the main assessment relationships.
•Configuration structure.Feature and extension settings relate
platform capabilities to organization and class contexts, allowing
supported tools to vary without changing the core academic data
model.
Design SignificanceThe relational structure separates institutional
membership, class participation, academic content, assessment, and feature
configuration while preserving the relationships required between them.
Intermediate membership and configuration entities are particularly
important because several EduVerse relationships depend on context rather
than simple ownership.
The ERD therefore provides the main design-level view of how
organizational governance and academic activity are represented within the
same data model.

5.4 Interface and Interaction Design
The EduVerse interface design reflects the role-aware and class-centered
structure established in the system model. Administrative, instructional,
and student-facing actions are presented through different workspace
contexts while maintaining consistent navigation and interaction patterns
across the platform.
The screenshots in this section show how these design principles appear
in the implemented web interface and demonstrate the resulting interaction
design.
5.4.1 Access and Identity Interfaces
Access and identity interfaces establish the organization and role context
used throughout the platform. Their design separates account authentication
from workspace selection and personal account settings so that users who
participate in multiple contexts can move between them without changing
account identity.

5.4.2 Administrative Governance Interfaces
Administrative interfaces group organization setup, membership,
permissions, class oversight, and feature configuration within a dedicated
governance context. This separation keeps institution-level controls distinct
from the day-to-day instructional activity that occurs inside classes.
The interface design also presents configurable options through structured
settings and management views rather than exposing the same controls to
every actor.

Chapter 6. Software and Engineering Implementation 109
6.1 Introduction
Chapter 5 described the structural design of EduVerse; this chapter explains
how that design was realized as an operational software system. It covers
the implementation of the web and mobile clients, shared server-side
services, persistence and file handling, authentication and authorization,
configurable features, real-time communication, AI support, the integrated
coding environment, and the engineering workflow used to integrate and
review changes.
The discussion focuses on implementation mechanisms and the distinct
workflow depth provided by the web and mobile clients.
6.2 Implementation Environment
The implementation environment comprises the browser and mobile clients,
the authenticated API layer, the database, and specialized external services
summarized in Table 6.1.
6.3 System Architecture
The implemented architecture follows a web-first, service-integrated cloud
model. Vercel hosts the deployed Next.js application, whose route handlers
and shared server libraries contain the server-side application logic for
authenticated workflows. The application integrates with managed services:
Supabase provides authentication, hosted PostgreSQL persistence, RPC
access, and selected realtime updates; AWS S3 stores binary files; LiveKit
provides live media infrastructure; and OpenRouter provides AI inference.
After authentication, the mobile companion interacts with the same
protected EduVerse service layer used by the web application. This keeps
access rules and workflow behavior centralized across both clients.
Protected client actions are resolved through the server layer, where
input validation, organization and role context, permissions, and workflow
conditions are applied before persistence or external-service operations are
performed. This structure keeps academic business rules server-owned while
allowing different clients to expose different levels of interaction.

Chapter 6. Software and Engineering Implementation 111
6.4 Web Application Implementation
The web application is implemented with the Next.js 16 App Router,
React 19, and TypeScript and serves as the primary operational client
of EduVerse. Tailwind CSS 4 and reusable Radix/shadcn-style interface
components support a consistent presentation layer. The application
structure combines role-aware routing with organization- and class-scoped
workspaces so that the active user context determines which interface and
server operations are available.
Web workflows interact with server-owned route handlers rather than
embedding academic business rules directly in presentation components.
Shared server utilities resolve authenticated context, validate requests, apply
access checks, and coordinate persistence or external-service operations.
The class workspace provides a common interaction shell for enabled
academic capabilities while preserving feature availability and role-specific
behavior. This allows the interface to remain consistent across classes
even when the available tools differ according to organization or class
configuration.
The App Router separates authenticated workspace routes from public
entry routes. Shared context providers supply application state and compose
the authenticated shell with live-session and exam-lock state.
6.5 Mobile Companion Application
Implementation
EduVerse Mobile is implemented with Expo, React Native, and TypeScript
as a companion to the primary web platform. Shared application state
is coordinated through the mobile provider layer, while domain operations
are accessed through a dedicated service layer that communicates with the
protected EduVerse backend.
Supabase provides mobile authentication and session persistence.
Its mobile client stores the session through AsyncStorage and refreshes
authentication tokens automatically. Authenticated service requests then
attach the current access token as a bearer token and reuse the platform’s
server-side academic workflows rather than reproducing the web application’s
business logic inside the mobile client.

Chapter 6. Software and Engineering Implementation 112
The mobile implementation provides authentication, organization
selection, class summaries, and notifications. It also provides material
access, class communication, profile utilities, and basic live-session
participation. The web client provides the broader administrative,
configuration, assessment-authoring, and whiteboard-centered live-session
workflows, while the mobile client focuses on high-frequency participation.
6.6 Backend, Database, and Storage
Implementation
EduVerse uses a Supabase-centered data layer coordinated by the Next.js
application rather than by a separate standalone backend application.
Next.js route handlers form the main application and API backend, while
shared server libraries perform request validation, authorization, workflow
execution, persistence, and integration with external services. Zod is used
for schema-based validation in selected structured request workflows.
Relational persistence is provided by Supabase-hosted PostgreSQL and
follows the domain structures documented in Chapter 5. Route handlers
access the required records where appropriate and invoke PostgreSQL
functions through Supabase RPC for centralized database operations. These
operations include evaluating class-management permissions, selecting the
active organization role, resolving feature availability, and coordinating
live-session claiming and lifecycle state.
Uploaded binary content is handled separately from relational academic
records. Supabase-hosted PostgreSQL stores academic records and
associated file metadata, while AWS S3 stores the binary content.
Server-side upload logic validates incoming files, writes permitted content
to S3 using protected credentials, and persists the corresponding metadata.
Protected downloads use signed URLs that expire after five minutes, while
material content can also be delivered through authenticated server-side
logic.
This server-mediated approach prevents storage credentials from being
exposed to clients and keeps file access subject to the authenticated academic
context of the surrounding workflow.

Chapter 6. Software and Engineering Implementation 113
6.7 Authentication, Authorization, and
Security
Authentication is implemented through Supabase Auth, including account
entry, recovery, session handling, and protected-route access. Authentication
establishes user identity, but protected EduVerse workflows also require
organization, role, membership, and class context to be resolved before
access is granted.
Authorization is applied through multiple implementation layers,
including authenticated application entry, server-side route checks,
active-role resolution, organization and class membership checks, and
database-level protections where configured. Shared authorization helpers
and permission RPCs keep these checks consistent across protected
workflows.
Row-Level Security policies defined in the database migrations provide
an additional access boundary for the schema areas to which those policies
are applied.
Additional security mechanisms include server-side input validation,
protected file access, controlled invitation and join workflows, role-sensitive
result visibility, exam passcode handling, integrity-event recording, and
platform audit logging.
6.8 Role-Based and Multi-Organization
Access
Multi-organization and multi-role access is implemented through
organization membership records, separate role associations, active-context
selection, and server-side access resolution. A single account can therefore
participate in more than one institutional context without requiring separate
identities.
When a protected workflow is opened, the implementation resolves the
active organization and role together with the relevant membership or class
relationship. Server-side access checks then determine whether the requested
action is permitted in that context.

6.9 Feature Availability and Extension
Implementation
Feature availability is implemented through shared definitions and
configuration records scoped to organization and class contexts. The
resolver combines definition defaults, organization settings, class settings,
and parent feature state. An organization-disabled capability cannot be
enabled by a class setting; a class can further disable a capability that
remains available to the organization.
The resolved configuration controls class navigation and feature exposure.
Database-side feature checks are also used in applicable protected workflows,
so the same configuration model can inform both application presentation
and server-controlled operations.
Extensions follow the same context-sensitive model. Organization
extension records define enabled extension entries, while class extension
settings can further restrict their exposure. Database validation prevents a
class from enabling an extension that is disabled for its organization.
6.10 Real-Time Communication and Live
Sessions
Real-time learning in EduVerse combines LiveKit-based media participation
with platform-managed session state. An authenticated server route verifies
class membership or management permission before issuing a room-scoped
LiveKit token, while Supabase records coordinate the active class session and
its lifecycle.
Session-state handling includes claiming or starting a session, marking it
live, ending it, and maintaining itslast_seen_atactivity timestamp. Host
clients send a heartbeat every 60 seconds, and server-side token and claim
logic uses a five-minute threshold when rejecting or replacing stale session
state. Supabase Realtime subscriptions propagate live-session record changes
to the application context.

6.11 AI Learning Support and IDE
Implementation
AI functionality is integrated through authenticated server-side routes
and supporting services that connect class context to OpenRouter, which
provides the AI inference layer. The default model for general generation
isnvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free. It supports contextual
class assistance, material study summarization, assignment support and
drafting, examination drafting, and feedback drafting. The default vision
model isgoogle/gemini-2.5-flash, which supports visual extraction when
image-based or visually rendered material requires vision processing. Both
defaults can be overridden through deployment-environment configuration.
Material processing does not rely exclusively on AI vision. Suitable PDF
content is processed through text extraction, while vision-based processing
is used when the material is image-based or depends on visual rendering.
AI access is subject to authenticated class context, class membership, and
management permission where required. For student-facing class assistance,
the system prompt instructs the model to guide learning without supplying
direct final answers to active assessments. This is a prompt-level academic
guardrail, not deterministic answer filtering.
The integrated development environment is a browser-oriented workspace
with a file tree, Monaco-based editing, project templates, virtual terminal
commands, persistent browser-local workspace state, and browser previews.
Templates cover Web, Python, C, C++, and SQL projects; however,
execution is intentionally constrained to client-side mechanisms. JavaScript
can execute in the browser, and Web and Markdown content can be
previewed. Python uses limited client-side interpretation or translation, C
and C++ behavior is simulated rather than native-compiled, and SQL uses
a restricted client-side simulation rather than a full database runtime. The
result is a browser-oriented coding environment with constrained client-side
execution rather than a collection of native language runtimes.

6.12 Development Workflow and
Deployment
Implementation changes were managed through version-controlled
branches or forks and pull-request review, supporting the feature-centered
development process described in Chapter 3. Merged pull-request commits
provide traceable integration of reviewed changes.
Three GitHub Actions workflows run on pushes and pull requests to the
main branch: a Next.js production build with Bun, a Biome formatting
check, and a TypeScript check usingtsc –noEmit. The EduVerse web
application is deployed through Vercel, and each pull request generates a
preview deployment that provides a running environment for reviewing
proposed changes before they are merged.
6.13 Implementation Challenges and
Adopted Solutions
Four recurring engineering challenges shaped the implementation:
•Multi-organization and multi-role authorization.Access
decisions had to remain correct across memberships and roles.
Selected context, shared authorization helpers, permission RPCs, and

•Cross-client consistency.Both clients needed consistent rules
without duplicated business logic. They reuse protected server
workflows while exposing different interface depths.
•Large-file handling.Binary files had to remain associated with
protected academic records without storing the binary content in
the relational database. Supabase-hosted PostgreSQL holds their
metadata, while server-controlled AWS S3 handles binary upload and
retrieval.

7.1 Introduction
Testing and evaluation examine whether the implemented EduVerse platform
behaves according to its academic, role-based, and technical responsibilities.
In a multi-organization educational system, correctness depends not only on
successful interface operation, but also on access control, assessment logic,
feature configuration, and other governed platform behavior.
This chapter summarizes the testing activities applied to EduVerse
and provides a concise evaluation of selected functional and non-functional
characteristics.
7.2 Testing Strategy
EduVerse was evaluated using automated logic-level testing together with
engineering verification during development. Automated tests focus on
rule-intensive platform behavior, while GitHub Actions verify production
builds, formatting, and TypeScript correctness. Vercel preview deployments
also support review of changes before merge.

The automated test suite covers selected rule-intensive areas of EduVerse,

Chapter 8. Future Work and Recommendations 122
8.1 Introduction
Future work for EduVerse focuses on two main directions: evaluating
scalability under broader real-world use and refining usability through
structured user feedback. These directions extend the project toward
evidence-basedperformanceplanninganduser-informedinterfacerefinement.
8.2 Scalability Improvements
As EduVerse is used by larger numbers of organizations, users, classes, files,
and live sessions, future evaluation can examine how the platform performs
under heavier and more concurrent workloads. This would help establish
practical performance baselines and identify areas that may require further
refinement as usage grows.
Operational monitoring can also be strengthened to provide clearer
information about system behavior, resource demand, and service reliability
during broader use. Such evidence would allow future scalability decisions to
be guided by observed platform behavior rather than assumed limitations.
8.3 User Feedback and Usability Refinement
A second direction is broader evaluation with Organization Administrators,
Teachers, and Students. Structured feedback from these user groups can
provide evidence about navigation clarity, workflow understanding, feature
discoverability, and the overall usability of the integrated platform.
Findings from usability testing, questionnaires, or other structured
feedback methods can then guide targeted refinements to interfaces and
workflows. The objective is to preserve the integrated nature of EduVerse
while keeping the experience clear, efficient, and manageable as the platform
evolves.
8.4 Chapter Summary
Future development can strengthen EduVerse through empirical scalability
evaluation, improved operational monitoring, and user-informed usability
refinement.

Conclusion
EduVerse was developed to address a clear problem in contemporary
digital education: closely related academic workflows often lack a shared
institutional context. This thesis has shown how a multi-organization,
role-based environment can coordinate learning management, live
collaboration, AI-driven support, and coding practice under common
governance.
The implemented system realizes this model through a primary web
platform, EduVerse Mobile support for selected high-frequency workflows,
protected shared APIs, role-aware access, and configurable services for data,
files, live sessions, and AI support. Both clients reuse the governed service
layer while providing interaction depth suited to their respective roles.
The project therefore contributes a coherent model for integrated digital
learning without sacrificing governance, extensibility, controlled feature
availability, or academic authority. Scalability, broader user feedback, and
continued usability refinement remain the principal next steps, while the
current implementation provides a practical foundation for that work.
